transcript.content: Hello. I'm glad you're here today. What brings you in to see me?

I feel like I’m constantly bracing myself—my whole body stays tight all day from worrying about my husband and everything I’m juggling. It has just become so overwhelming trying to manage his health issues alongside all of my usual commitments.
Did this constant worry and physical tension start specifically when your husband's health issues began, or have you felt this way about various areas of your life for at least six months?

It has been going on for about seven months now, starting shortly after my husband's health issues settled into a long-term routine. While it began with his health, the worry has definitely spread to other areas, like worrying about letting people down at the art center or how we will manage financially if his medications change.
How difficult is it for you to control or stop these worries once they start, even when you try to focus on other things?

It is incredibly difficult to stop them once they start, even when I try to tell myself to stop. The "what-ifs" just keep barging back in, and I'll find I've reread the same page in a book three times because my mind has wandered off to worry about his heart or his next appointment. It feels like I have no control over where my thoughts go.
Along with the muscle tension and trouble concentrating, have you also been experiencing sleep problems, feeling easily fatigued, or feeling unusually irritable over these past seven months?

Yes, I've been feeling extremely fatigued for the last seven months, like I'm constantly moving through molasses even when I get a full night of sleep. Sleep itself isn't really the issue, and I haven't noticed feeling unusually irritable, but this physical exhaustion is very real and constant.
Before your husband's health issues began, did you tend to worry a lot about everyday things, or is this level of constant anxiety completely new to you?

I'm not entirely sure what my past worrying habits were like, but this level of constant, overwhelming anxiety is definitely new to me. It really only started after my husband's illness and taking on all these new responsibilities.
Do you find yourself also worrying excessively about minor, everyday things that others might not think twice about, like being slightly late, minor chores, or small daily mishaps?

Yes, I definitely do. Even the smallest hiccup, like a simple text from the clinic or second-guessing how I organized my husband's daily pills, feels like it could snowball into a major disaster. I also worry excessively about letting people down at the art center over minor schedule changes, which just sets me on edge for hours.
Have you recently been diagnosed with any medical conditions, like thyroid issues, or started any new medications that could be contributing to your anxiety and fatigue?

No, I haven't been diagnosed with any new medical conditions like thyroid issues, and I'm not taking any new medications myself. The only new medications I deal with are the ones I'm managing for my husband's health conditions.
Over the past seven months, have these worries and physical tension been present on most days, or have you had periods of a few weeks where you felt completely free from them?

Yes, they have been present almost every single day over the past seven months. I haven't had any weeks or even a few days where I felt completely free from the worry and tension. It has been a constant, daily presence ever since my husband's health issues settled into a routine.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with excessive, uncontrollable anxiety and worry about multiple everyday domains (husband's health, finances, commitments at the art center, and minor daily tasks) for a duration of 7 months, occurring almost daily. The worry is accompanied by significant physical and cognitive symptoms, including persistent muscle tension, severe fatigue, and concentration difficulties. The presentation meets the full diagnostic criteria for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1) and is not attributable to a substance or GMC, ruling out adjustment disorder as the primary diagnosis due to the generalized nature, severity, and symptom profile of the anxiety.
